rashi:a2.1: Not in his presence: like this one, who was hiding. And because there are two drawbacks, that it is not in his presence and that it is against his will, for that reason Hillel needed to institute [the ordinance].
rashi:a4.1: [Hillel] instituted what was needed: and even if the buyer had been there and had not wanted to accept [the money], Hillel would have needed to institute that [giving] against his will is giving.
rashi:a6.1: Gemara. House: “then the house that is in the city shall stand” (Leviticus 25:30).
rashi:a6.2: Towers: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss), and fixed in the ground.
rashi:a6.3: The verse states “house”: and those listed above resemble a house.
rashi:a8.1: A quarry: the difference between them is a place that is not fit for sowing. For Rabbi Meir does not mean actual fields, since “house” is written there; rather, he includes a quarry and a sand bed, which resemble a house, since they are not fit for sowing and are suited to building a house: a quarry, to take stones from there, and a sand bed, to take sand from it. And Rabbi Yehuda holds that they resemble fields.
rashi:a8.2: And it is taught: [said] as a support [not as a challenge].
rashi:a9.1: In accordance with the simple meaning of the verse: for we see that her house was within the wall, and it says “and she dwelt upon the wall,” that is to say, she dwelt in a walled city.
rashi:a10.1: Mishna. Whose roofs are its wall: they did not surround it with a wall, but surrounded it with houses, and the houses are pressed one against another like a wall.
rashi:a10.2: Three courtyards: [a place with three courtyards,] in each of which there are two houses, is called a city.
rashi:a10.3: Katzra: the name of a small city outside Tzippori.
rashi:a11.1: Gemara. Shur iggar [a wall of roofs]: [a city] whose roofs are its wall.
rashi:a12.1: Lo a wall: lo is written [lamed-vav-alef]; it implies lo, “not,” and it implies lo, “to it.” That is to say, it does not have [a wall] now but it had a wall before; [a house in it,] too, is transferred in perpetuity.
rashi:a13.1: What is he saying: is there no city surrounded by a wall in the Galilee except Gamla, and in Transjordan except Gedod?
tosafot:a1.1: In brief: Tosafot ask: why would one need a proof that giving against the recipient’s will is not giving? It is obvious that a person need not accept a gift against his will; and how, then, could Rav Pappa disagree? They answer: a voluntary gift that the giver has no need to give is certainly not giving against the recipient’s will, and Rav Pappa does not disagree about that. They disagree only about a gift that the giver needs to give, as here, where he said “This is your bill of divorce on the condition that you give me two hundred zuz,” and she needs to give in order to fulfill the condition of the bill of divorce; and as with the payment in our mishna. But where the giver is obligated, as with a debt or a deposit, giving against the recipient’s will is certainly giving, as in Bava Kamma (118a): one who lent to another or deposited with him in a settled place may not return it to him in the desert, which implies that in a settled place he returns it to him even against his will. They ask further from Gittin (74a): “This is your bill of divorce on the condition that you give me my cloak,” and the cloak was lost: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says she gives its value. From the dilemma in the Gemara there (where the husband said “the two hundred zuz are forgiven to you”) Tosafot show that the case speaks of payment against the husband’s will, so Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that giving against his will is giving; how then can Rava say here that it is not? They answer that according to Rava, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel speaks there of payment with the husband’s consent, and the dilemma there is not according to Rava, for whom, according to the Rabbis, even “they are forgiven to you” does not help. They ask: according to Rava, who holds that even in the city giving against the recipient’s will is not giving, why did the buyer need to hide? Let him say “I do not accept,” and it is not giving, and the house becomes his after twelve months. They answer: had he been in the city, he would have been ashamed not to accept. Last, it is implied that according to Rava even in his presence giving against his will is not giving; how can he prove this from Hillel’s ordinance, which was made only for payment not in the buyer’s presence, as Rav Pappa objects? They answer: if giving in his presence against his will were giving, Hillel would not have needed to institute, for a case not in his presence, that the seller place his money in the chamber, since it could be acquired on the buyer’s behalf through another person; rather, from the fact that Hillel needed to institute that giving against his will is giving, conclude that in general it is not. Rav Pappa, who objects, does not hold this reasoning. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a8.1: A quarry: Rashi explains: to take stones from there, and a sand bed, to take sand from there. And the Rashbam explained in Bava Batra (67a): ḥolasit, to take glass from it; and metzula, as in “a metzula of fish” (Berakhot 9b) [a deep pool].
tosafot:a12.1: Which has a wall: Rashi explains that lo is written [lamed-vav-alef], implying “to it” and implying “not”; that is, it does not have [a wall] now but it had one before. But it is not so: in precise Ḥumashim it is written lo with an alef, and read with a vav. [Another printed reading has: with a vav, and not read with an alef.]
tosafot:a13.1: What is he saying: is there no city surrounded by a wall in the Galilee except Gamla, and in Transjordan except Gedod? And if you say: why does he not ask the same of the mishna? One can say that he rightly asks it of the baraita, because it is more precise, stating explicitly Gamla in the Galilee and Gedod in Transjordan.
gershom:a1.1: And therefore he needed to institute giving not in his presence, as with this one [who places his money in the chamber].
gershom:a2.1: And Hillel instituted what he needed. But in general, whether in his presence or not in his presence: with his consent, yes; against his will, no.
gershom:a3.1: Anything within the wall, such as olive-press houses, bathhouses, towers, dovecotes and everything like them: these are like the houses of walled cities and are transferred in perpetuity along with it after twelve months.
gershom:a4.1: Except for the fields: for if there are fields within the city, they are not transferred in perpetuity.
gershom:a5.1: House: as it is written: “Then the house that is in the city that has [a wall] shall stand.”
gershom:a6.1: Only a house: which is a dwelling house, which is transferred in perpetuity.
gershom:a7.1: The verse states “house”: what resembles a house, to exclude fields. These are the words of Rabbi Yehuda.
gershom:a8.1: But [according to] Rabbi Meir, isn’t “house” written, which implies that what resembles a house is transferred in perpetuity, but not a field?
gershom:a10.1: And metzula: simply a deep place that has water. These are not fit for sowing, and they do not so much resemble a dwelling house. According to Rabbi Yehuda, who excludes fields, he also excludes these, which resemble a field, since there is no dwelling in them. According to Rabbi Meir, who wants to include even fields, he cannot include actual fields, because “house” is written; but a quarry and a sand bed, which resemble a house, like a tower and a pit, he indeed holds are transferred in perpetuity along with it.
gershom:a11.1: And it is taught: a support.
gershom:a12.1: A house built into the city wall: Rabbi Yehuda says it is not transferred in perpetuity like the houses of walled cities, because it is as though it stands outside the city.
gershom:a13.1: Rabbi Shimon says: the outer wall of the house is its wall, and it is like a tower that stands in the wall, and it is transferred in perpetuity.
gershom:a14.1: Rabbi Shimon holds in accordance with the simple meaning of the verse: as it implies, “for her house was upon the side of the wall,” and even so, “and she dwelt upon the wall,” meaning within the wall.
gershom:a15.1: And Rabbi Yehuda holds: “she dwelt upon the wall” is written, and not in a walled city; that is to say, it is not like [a house] within the wall. [A parenthetical in the text reads: some say, she dwelt on its roofs.]
gershom:a16.1: A city whose roofs are its walls: some say that the whole wall around is full of roofs, and some say that its roofs slope down to the ground, and they are the walls.
gershom:a17.1: Wall: as it is written, “that has a wall around.” We require [an actual] wall around the city, and not a shur iggar, a wall of roofs.
gershom:a18.1: Around: as it is written: “But the houses of the villages that have no wall around them.” By inference, the houses of walled cities require a wall all around.
gershom:a19.1: Which has [lo] a wall: it is written with an alef; that is to say, even though it does not have [a wall] now, if it had one before, it is judged like the houses of walled cities.
gershom:b1.1: Old Katzra, which is within the boundary of Tzippori.
gershom:b2.1: Until Gamla in the Galilee: that is to say, all the towns in the Galilee that are larger than Gamla, up to and including Gamla (for Gamla had three courtyards of two houses each), and that are surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua son of Nun, are judged like the houses of walled cities; to exclude those smaller than Gamla, [which are not so judged]. And likewise until Gedod in Transjordan; and Ḥadid and Ono and Jerusalem in Judea: all those as large as them or larger, and surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua son of Nun, are judged like the houses of walled cities. Rava said: when the baraita teaches “Gamla in the Galilee,” it is to exclude a Gamla in other lands, which is not surrounded [by a wall] from the days of Joshua; and likewise not Gedod of other lands. And those others, Katzra, Ḥakra and Yodfat, which are surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua: since there are none like them in other lands bearing these names and not surrounded by a wall, he did not need to mention them in the Tosefta [the baraita].
gershom:b3.1: Ten matters were stated with regard to Jerusalem: they are detailed in chapter Merubeh [Bava Kamma 82b].
gershom:b4.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan said: like Jerusalem: that is to say, we require [a city] like Jerusalem, that it be surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua son of Nun; but not like Jerusalem itself, in which a house is not transferred in perpetuity, since it belongs to all Israel.
gershom:b5.1: While here: with regard to these places that we mentioned.
gershom:b6.1: There were two [places called] Kadesh: in tractate Makkot, in chapter Elu Hen HaGolin.
gershom:b7.1: Why did the Sages count these: Yodfat and Gamla, and so on.
gershom:b8.1: And they sanctified them for the Sabbatical Year and the Jubilees, for tithes, and for the law of the houses of walled cities.
gershom:b9.1: But the first ones: which had already been sanctified and were surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua, their sanctity was nullified when the [sanctity of the] land was nullified, when they were exiled.
gershom:b10.1: Since he says “they sanctified them,” he holds that the first consecration: [that is,] with which Joshua sanctified them.
gershom:b11.1: Sanctified it for its time: all the time that they were in it, until [the time of the destruction].
gershom:b12.1: And did not sanctify it for the future: that [sanctity] does not apply when they returned from the exile.
gershom:b13.1: And were these alone, mentioned above, surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua? But it is already [stated: “sixty cities,” and so on, and it is written: “all these were fortified with high walls”].
gershom:b14.1: But we say below that there is no need to sanctify them: as it says, because the first consecration sanctified it for its time and sanctified it for the future.
gershom:b15.1: Rather, they found these, which had not changed from what they had been, [and counted them for their halakhot].
gershom:b16.1: All these mitzvot: that apply in towns surrounded by a wall [from the days of Joshua] apply in them, as we learned in [the order of] Tohorot: “Towns surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua son of Nun are holier than it [the rest of the land].”
gershom:b17.1: Two tannaim, and according to Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei: one says it sanctified for the future, and one says it did not sanctify.
gershom:b18.1: “Which has [lo] a wall,” even though it does not have one now: for it is not written “and it had a wall,” but “which has [lo],” implying that even if it had [one] before, it is counted among walled cities. Evidently he holds that the first consecration sanctified for its time and sanctified for the future.
gershom:b19.1: With the renewal of all these matters: [evidently] they needed to sanctify a second time.
gershom:b20.1: And the other: the one who says it sanctified for the future too, how does he explain “And all the congregation of those that were coming back made [sukkot and dwelt in sukkot]”?
gershom:b21.1: He holds that it does not speak of actual sukkot, but that Ezra’s merit protected them like a sukka, because he nullified the inclination of idol worship from them, as we explain in tractate Sanhedrin, in chapter Arba Mitot.
gershom:b22.1: And this is why the verse is exacting with him: for it shortens [his name] and calls him Yeshua, because he did not pray for mercy and did not nullify the inclination of idol worship.
gershom:b23.1: And according to this tanna, isn’t it written “which your fathers possessed and you shall possess it,” comparing: so too your possession comes with the renewal of all the matters, so evidently it needs to be sanctified, since it did not sanctify for the future? This is what it says: he will tell you that he expounds the verse thus: since your fathers possessed it, you [too] possess it with that very same sanctity, and you do not need another consecration.
gershom:b24.1: The whole congregation together was four myriads [and more]: for not even a tenth of Israel were in their places, as we have a tradition that Israel is never fewer than sixty myriads; all the more so they did not count Jubilees.
gershom:b25.1: And they were intermingled: in the allotment, the tribe of Judah in Benjamin.
gershom:b26.1: [The text here reads “Rav Yitzḥak said”; the daf has Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak.] They counted Jubilees for the need of sanctifying Sabbatical Years, [since the Sabbatical Years were not nullified, only the Jubilees, and so they would count Jubilees in order to sanctify Sabbatical Years] in their time. Since the Jubilee year is not counted among the years of the seven-year cycle, they needed to count and to know when the Jubilee is, since the Jubilee comes after seven Sabbatical cycles, and they must make the eighth Sabbatical Year after eight years, since the Jubilee year does not count toward the Sabbatical reckoning.
rashi:b1.1: Until Gamla: all the towns in the Galilee as far as Gamla were surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua.
rashi:b2.1: Rava said: this tanna comes to explain our mishna, and this is what he says: the Gamla that our mishna teaches was surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua is the Gamla of the Galilee.
rashi:b2.2: To exclude: that if there is a Gamla in Transjordan or in Judea, it was not surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua. And likewise Gedod. And likewise Ḥadid and Jerusalem in Judea: to exclude towns in the Galilee and in Transjordan called Ḥadid, Ono and Jerusalem, which are not surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua.
rashi:b2.3: Those that have none like them: those that [the tanna] counts in our mishna, such as Katzra and Yodfat, which have no namesakes elsewhere; the baraita did not need to teach in which land they stand.
rashi:b3.1: Ten matters: they are explained in Bava Kamma, in chapter Merubeh (Bava Kamma 82b), and this is one of them.
rashi:b3.2: A house is not transferred in perpetuity: because it is written (Leviticus 25:30) “to the one who bought it, throughout his generations,” and he holds that Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes; so who would transfer it to him?
rashi:b4.1: Didn’t Rav Yosef say, and so on: in tractate Makkot, in chapter Elu Hen HaGolin (Makkot 10a).
rashi:b5.1: These: those enumerated in our mishna.
rashi:b5.2: And they sanctified them: it is explained in tractate Shevuot (16a) that one sanctifies it with two thanksgiving offerings and with song, and the court walks, with the two thanksgiving offerings behind them, and so on.
rashi:b5.3: Were nullified: for the sanctity of the land does not apply in them, and the law of walled cities does not apply in them.
rashi:b5.4: When the sanctity of the land was nullified: at the first destruction.
rashi:b5.5: The first consecration: with which Joshua sanctified it.
rashi:b6.1: But you say: below, at the end, that this is a matter that does not need to be sanctified, as it teaches in the latter clause: “And not only these, but any that comes into your hand, and so on,” for it sanctified it for its time and for the future.
rashi:b8.1: One of them: this one, which teaches that it sanctified it for the future, Rabbi Elazar bar Yosei said it, just as he says “even though it does not have [a wall] now”: although it is destroyed, its sanctity is not nullified.
rashi:b10.1: Rather, it compares their arrival in the days of Ezra, and so on: for “they had not done so” does not refer back to the sukkot; rather, this is what it says: they had not done what they did now since the days of Joshua. And what is that? The consecration of the land.
rashi:b10.2: They counted Sabbatical Years: they began to count Sabbatical Years and became obligated in tithes.
rashi:b11.1: And the Lord your God will bring you, and so on: the verse speaks of their return from the exile, as it is written just before it (Deuteronomy 30:3): “Then the Lord your God will turn your captivity and have compassion upon you.”
rashi:b12.1: And the other: actually “they had not done so” does refer to the sukkot, but not actual sukkot; rather, Ezra prayed for mercy regarding the inclination of idol worship and it was delivered into his hands, as it says in Sanhedrin (64a).
rashi:b12.2: And the merit protected: [the merit] of Ezra, over them.
rashi:b12.3: Like a sukka: for they had not done this thing so in the days of Joshua. And this is why the verse is exacting to mention Joshua more than the others, and mentions him in a derogatory form.
rashi:b13.1: For everywhere “Yehoshua” is written, and here “Yeshua”: because he should have prayed for mercy about the matter; for granted, Moses did not pray for mercy, and so on.
rashi:b14.1: You possess it: with that same sanctity, and there is no need to sanctify it again.
rashi:b15.1: When the tribe of Reuben were exiled: in the days of Sennacherib.
rashi:b18.1: They counted Jubilees to sanctify Sabbatical Years: certainly the Jubilee was not in effect, such that slaves would go free because of the Jubilee or sold fields would return; but the Sabbatical Years were in effect, to cancel debts and to cease from sowing and harvesting. For they needed to count the Jubilee year so that the Sabbatical Years would come in their proper place: at the end of seven Sabbatical cycles they would leave aside the fiftieth year and not count it toward the next Sabbatical cycle, since it is fit to be a Jubilee year, and the count begins with the year after it. For if they did not count Jubilees, they would count that year in the reckoning of the Sabbatical cycles, and the Sabbatical Years would fall out of their place.
tosafot:b4.1: Here too there were two Jerusalems: and it is puzzling, for according to Rava too we need to say this, that there were two Jerusalems. One can say that according to Rava we need not say that there were two Jerusalems in Judea, only in other lands; but according to Rav Ashi we must say that there were two Jerusalems in Judea.
tosafot:b10.1: And they sanctified walled cities: meaning, with regard to the sale of a house among the houses of walled cities, and with regard to sending lepers outside the city. For only in walled cities must lepers be sent outside the wall, but not in other [cities]; whereas afflicted stones must be sent outside the city even if [it] was not surrounded [by a wall] from the days of Joshua. And so it is taught in Torat Kohanim: “them … outside the city” [of the stones]; but a person is not [sent] outside every city, only outside cities surrounded by a wall. And if you say: from where do we derive this? “A walled house” is not written with regard to a leper! Our master Rabbeinu Yitzḥak says that we derive “outside the camp shall his dwelling [moshavo] be,” written of the leper (Leviticus 13:46), from “dwelling” written in “a dwelling house in a walled city” (Leviticus 25:29). And Rashi explains here that it is sanctified with two thanksgiving offerings and with song, and the court walking with two thanksgiving offerings behind them, as in Shevuot (16a). And in tractate Shevuot Rashi explains that we find they would sanctify the walls of Jerusalem with two thanksgiving offerings and with song when they came to add to the city and to the courtyards; but other cities, I do not know how they would sanctify them.
tosafot:b18.1: In brief: This raises a difficulty against a baraita in the Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Gittin, which Rashi cites in chapter HaSholeiaḥ (Gittin 36a): “And this is the manner of the remission: remitting”: the verse speaks of two remissions, the remission of the Jubilee and the remission of the Sabbatical Year; when you remit in the Jubilee you remit in the Sabbatical Year, and when you do not remit in the Jubilee you do not remit in the Sabbatical Year. Yet here it says that they counted Jubilees only to sanctify Sabbatical Years [so the Sabbatical Year was observed without the Jubilee]. Rashi explained in HaSholeiaḥ that [the Sabbatical Year spoken of in] Arakhin is rabbinic; but Torat Kohanim does not imply so [a parenthetical adds Rashi’s words: “and I say it is a dispute of tannaim,” since the Jerusalem Talmud’s baraita is Rabbi’s]. Further, Rabbeinu Tam says that the baraita cited at the beginning of HaSholeiaḥ reads the two remissions as the remission of land and the remission of money; the Jerusalem Talmud’s baraita is Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi], and the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi and say: from where is it derived that there is a Sabbatical Year even when there is no Jubilee? The verse states: “And you shall count seven sabbaths of years” (Leviticus 25:8); and from where that one makes a Jubilee even when there is no Sabbatical Year? The verse states: “forty-nine years.” Our passage follows the Rabbis. Still, Torat Kohanim can be reconciled even according to Rabbi: “a Sabbatical Year even when there is no Jubilee” can mean even when they did not observe the Jubilee and stayed in their sin, as taught in Rosh HaShana (9b): “It is a Jubilee” even if they did not release and even if they did not blow the shofar; might it be so even if they did not free [slaves]? The verse says “it is,” the words of Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yosei says: it is a Jubilee even if they did not release and even if they did not free; might it be so even if they did not blow? The verse says “it is.” Open on Sefaria for the full text.
